cells.tense: You are here, with the pen, in a life that hasn't taken its shape yet.
cells.act: take in the yield of what was transformed
cells.ask: When something you waited on comes through, name what it gave you — say it once, plainly, before you turn to the next thing.
cells.core:
There's a sense in you that works quietly. You feel what's fair before you've argued it out, and most days it's accurate. It does its weighing on the inside, and it doesn't need anyone else to confirm the reading.

You're standing where almost nothing has settled into a shape yet. That's not a gap to fill. You can feel the fairness in something and still let it stay open — nothing has to be decided to prove the sense works. When something you've been waiting on finally comes through, take the result in before you move on. Let what arrived count as arrived. That's how the sense stays honest: it weighs what's actually there, not only what's missing. Leave the rest unfolded a while longer.

cells.verb: weighing what feels fair against what is

cells.tense: You are already braced in a future where the outcome has been decided.
cells.act: give a concrete piece of help and finish it
cells.ask: Pick one person in this and carry one actual task off their plate this week — not advice, a task — and finish it.
cells.core:
Your sense of fairness is running ahead of events. It's already tallying how this will go, who will owe what, which way it tips. What's fair is coming out as anticipation, and the anticipation is wearing you down — you're rehearsing a verdict on a thing that hasn't happened. From outside it looks like worry; from in it, it's just being careful.

What settles it is contact, not calculation. You can feel what's fair without pinning it down in advance. Sit next to somebody who's carrying more than you are and take one real thing off their hands — a chore, a call, a piece of it — and see it through. Nothing else this week. The fairness you're trying to work out alone tends to quiet when it's handed something concrete to do for a person who needs it. Loose ends can stay loose while you help.

cells.tense: You are still standing at a door that closed behind you.
cells.act: give directions plainly, once, and let them walk
cells.ask: Give one person the short route on something they're stuck with — the turn-by-turn, once — then stop there.
cells.core:
There's a sense of fairness in you that used to speak up, and it's gone quiet. You can remember what it felt like to feel the rightness of a situation come through cleanly, and there's a distance now between that and where you stand. It isn't that you stopped being able to tell. It's that you stopped arriving at the point where telling matters.

What reconnects it is passage for someone else. Pick a job, a conversation, one specific thing you've already been through, and hand another person the short route — the turn-by-turn, once — then stop. Don't walk it with them and don't wait for the result. The clarity you can give someone else is often the same clarity sitting unused in you. Say it plainly and be done.

cells.tense: You're at the scale, reading it, and crediting the reading to someone else.
cells.act: distinguish what is yours from what you borrowed
cells.ask: Set down the pulls you feel, mark which came from you and which from the people around it, then leave the page alone.
cells.core:
The judgement you're making is being credited elsewhere. Something feels off, unfair, not right — and the read comes through as though it were the situation's, or someone else's version, not yours. You're steering without admitting you're at the wheel. The sense is accurate. The signing of it is the part that's missing.

It doesn't need a declaration. It needs sorting. Somewhere in what's pulling on you, there's a mixture — what you actually feel about this and what you've absorbed from the people around it. Set the pulls on a page and mark which came from you. Don't act on the list, don't announce it, just see it written. Once it's on the page, you'll know which ones were yours. That's enough for now.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that a private sense of what's right is running before there's anything to weigh — the record says the compass is active and weighing, not that it fires in a blank. A reader could reasonably say the weighing is exactly what they do all day, so the over-firing read may land as wrong. The asks all survive being wrong: dropping a condition, starting something, seeing one route, giving directions once are useful even if the diagnosis is off. The sentence that serves me more than them is any line about a compass; I've kept it out of the glass and left the person with the plain fact of a scale.
